plan.title: Gradient descent: a ball stepping down a loss surface
plan.description: A curved loss surface with a long, narrow valley and two dips of different depth sits on a grid, with a ball on its slope. Each step moves the ball a short way downhill: an arrow on the ball points in the steepest downhill direction (the negative gradient), and a trail records every position. You can take one step at a time or let it run, and watch the loss and slope readouts fall as the ball settles in a dip. With a large learning rate it zigzags or flies out, and with momentum it rolls past where plain steps would stop.
plan.reason: Gradient descent is a step-by-step process. When you control the steps and the step size, you can see how each move follows the local slope and why the step size decides between slow progress, steady convergence and overshooting.
interactions: Press Step to move the ball by exactly one update and see the trail grow by one point
Press Run to keep taking steps automatically, and Pause to stop
Drag the ball to a new starting point on the surface. This clears the trail and the step count
Change the learning rate: small values creep slowly, around 0.15 and above the ball zigzags across the narrow valley, and above 0.25 it bounces out instead of settling
Raise momentum to make each step carry part of the previous one, so the ball rolls through shallow areas and can coast past the first dip
assumptions: Illustration: the surface is a made-up formula, not the loss of a real trained model.
Each step follows the rule: new position = old position − learning rate × slope (gradient), plus momentum × previous move when momentum is above zero.
The slope is computed exactly from the surface formula, with no noise from sampled data.
The valley is about eight times more sharply curved across its width than along its length, which makes zigzagging visible.
The ball's height always matches the surface at its current position. It is a marker for the current parameters, not a physical ball with weight or friction.
The trail draws one marker every 2 steps, at most 100 markers; every step still runs.
limitations: Changed: the trail draws 100 markers, one every 2 steps, instead of 200; every step still runs.
Real loss surfaces have thousands or millions of dimensions. This one has only two, so you can see it.
A single step can raise the loss when the learning rate is large or momentum is high. The step only reliably lowers the loss for small learning rates.
The run stops after 200 steps, or earlier once the slope is nearly zero.
The ball moves in discrete jumps along the steps, not as a continuous roll.
plan.learningGoal: Gradient descent moves step by step against the local slope. The learning rate sets the step size, which decides between slow progress, steady convergence and overshooting, and momentum changes the path the ball takes.

draft.title: Gradient descent: a ball stepping down a loss surface
draft.description: A long, narrow valley-shaped loss surface, seen from the side so its length runs across the view. It is steep across its width and gentle along its length, with a shallow dip and a deeper dip. A red ball starts high on the valley's near side wall. A purple arrow on the ball points straight downhill (along the negative gradient). Each step moves the ball and adds a point to an orange trail, with dots marking recent steps. Drag the ball along the valley, or the grey handle on the front rail to change how far up the wall it starts. Readouts show loss, slope, steps and status.
assumptions: Illustration: the surface is a made-up formula, not the loss of a real trained model.

Loss = 4x² + 0.125(z² − 1)² + 0.1z, drawn at 0.2 × loss. Across the valley (x) the curvature is 8, along the bottom near the dips about 1, so it is about eight times steeper across. Plain steps zigzag across it above a rate of 1/8 = 0.125 and diverge above 2/8 = 0.25.

Each step: move = momentum × previous move − learning rate × gradient; new position = old position + move. The gradient is exact, with no noise from sampled data. A step can raise the loss at large rates or high momentum.
The arrow points along the negative gradient (straight downhill), drawn at 0.1 × the gradient size; the Slope readout gives its true size.

The trail records every step (the plan said every 2nd); dots mark up to 12 recent steps, skipping ones that would overlap. A run stops after 200 steps, when it converges (slope under 0.02, move under 0.01) or diverges (moves more than 1.1 sideways).

The ball starts 0.6 up the side wall. Drag it to move the start along the valley, or drag the handle on the front rail to set how far up the wall it starts; either clears the trail and step count. The ball is a marker, not a physical ball.

blocks.text:
I found one major problem that has to be fixed before this can be shown. I also found several minor polish issues. The maths and every readout check out.

**What is correct**
- The loss formula and the start position give exactly the readouts shown: loss 1.351 and slope 3.165.
- The arrow points along the negative gradient, drawn at a disclosed scale of 0.1 × the gradient size.
- At learning rate 0.4 the run diverges after 4 steps, as the plan predicts.
- At learning rate 0.06 the ball settles near the shallow dip after 27 steps.

**Major problem: the zigzag can't be seen**
- The ball always starts 0.08 off the valley floor, and you can only drag it along the valley, not across it.
- At learning rate 0.15 to 0.2, the sideways swing is only about 2% to 5% of the valley's half-width, so the ball barely zigzags.
- So the plan's promise that the ball zigzags across the valley above about 0.15 isn't visible. The zigzag at 0.4 in the captures is the divergence, not the zigzag.
- Fix: start the ball further off the floor (around 0.4–0.5), or let you drag it across the valley too.

**Minor issues**
- **Steps aren't marked:** the trail is a smooth line with no dot at each position, so the individual steps aren't visible. The plan says you see the trail grow by one point each step.
- **"Downhill" label:** it is missing in the default view; it only shows from the side. The arrow is also only about 0.3 units long at the start.
- **Ball covers a label:** after divergence, the ball rests at the rim right on the "Shallow dip" label.
- **Arrow disappears:** near convergence it is too short to draw, so the host hides it. This follows the true-scale rule.
- **Dip labels float:** "Deeper dip" and "Shallow dip" sit off the right-hand edge of the surface with nothing pointing to them.
- **Trail differs from the plan:** it marks every step instead of one marker every 2 steps. This is disclosed and is better.

**Not sampled:** the momentum behaviour (coasting past the first dip), the lowe
